name: A product's life cycle and where it is made
idea: An open textbook states that the work's theory gives a product life cycle three stages: new, maturing and standardized. It states that the theory assumed a new product is made entirely in the home country where it was invented. As an example of the last stage, it names a product that is now standardized and mostly made in low-cost countries.
suggests: Look at how mature a company's product is and where it is made: whether production stays near where the product was invented, or has begun to move to lower-cost countries as the product became standard.
limits: The textbook states that the theory explains today's trade patterns, in which innovation and manufacturing occur around the world, less well; global companies even locate research and development work in developing markets, where highly skilled staff and facilities usually cost less.
competing_idea: The same textbook describes another theory, which focuses on multinational firms and their efforts to win a competitive advantage over other global firms in their industry, and says that what it calls the barriers to entry are the critical ways for firms to gain a lasting competitive advantage.
questions: Is the product new, maturing or standardized, and has the way it is made settled?
Has production moved, or begun to move, from the country where the product was invented to lower-cost countries?
Does the company also do research and development abroad, where skilled staff and facilities may cost less?

originals.reference: International Business, Saylor Academy, section 2.1 "What Is International Trade Theory?" (an open textbook)
originals.about: Raymond Vernon, "International Investment and International Trade in the Product Cycle", The Quarterly Journal of Economics, vol. 80, issue 2, 1966, pp. 190-207
